newsitem.title: FRANCE: French transit strike flops on reform anniversary.
newsitem.headline: French transit strike flops on reform anniversary.

text.p: Trade unions hoping to rekindle last year's labour unrest over unpopular government welfare reforms suffered a setback on Friday when a public transport strike called for Paris failed to materialise.
Friday's action was intended to crown a low-key week of protests called by the Communist-led CGT union to demand wage increases, protest against job cuts and urge a halt to privatisation.

But city transport officials said the Paris Metro underground was running at least 70 percent of normal services while buses were running at 90 percent and suburban RER trains were virtually unaffected.

However a last-minute strike call by pilots' unions at Air France Europe, part of the Air France group, succeeded in grounding 60 percent of the carrier's scheduled flights, an airline spokeswoman said.
The 48-hour strike called by the USPNT, SPIT, SNPNAC and SPNL unions to protest at planned job cuts "is being widely followed", the spokeswoman added.
Flights to Corsica and Strasbourg were being maintained but newly created shuttle services between Paris and the southern cities of Marseille, Nice and Toulon had to be dropped.

An internal notice circulated by the airline's press office branded the strike "sabotage" and accused pilots of defending their own selfish interests at a time when new shuttle flights between major cities were drawing new passengers.

Many regional newspapers failed to appear on Friday after a one-day journalists' strike on Thursday called in protest at government plans to scrap a tax break for media employees and 100 other professions.
A last-minute printers' strike also robbed newstands of nine national dailies that had hoped to publish despite the strike.

The strikes coincide with calls by major French unions for new protests on the first anniversary of a controversial welfare reform plan unveiled by conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe on November 15, 1995.
But protests were insignificant compared to those last year, when crippling transport and public sector strikes virtually paralysed France for more than three weeks.

CGT leader Louis Viannet said the protests were not as big as they had been a year ago but said workers were still angry because Juppe's reforms had done nothing to reverse record unemployment of 12.6 percent or end welfare system deficits.
"We are witnessing mounting anger which will manifest itself in additional demonstrations tomorrow and in the weeks to come," Viannet said in a radio interview on France Inter.
Divisions over policy and strategy have taken their toll on union strength since Juppe's welfare reforms last year.
The pro-Socialist CFDT, France's biggest union, has refused to take part in Friday's anniversary protest because it backed last year's reforms.
